Rethinking Local News: How Sarah Alvarez Is Building Journalism in Support of Community Needs

Nieman Reports · 2026-11-11 13:00 UTC

Sarah Alvarez has spent much of her career rethinking how local journalism can serve the public. After working as a civil rights attorney, then as a reporter and producer at the NPR station Michigan Public, she founded Outlier Media in 2016. Alvarez said the Detroit-based nonprofit newsroom was designed to fill information and accountability gaps in communities that were often overlooked by traditional news organizations.. One of its signature innovations, TXT OUTLIER, is a text message service Alvarez created to connect Detroiters directly with journalists and provide practical information on issues affecting their lives, from utility bills to housing and foreclosures. Under Alvarez’s leadership, Outlier also expanded its Documenters program, an initiative that trains and pays residents to attend and report on public meetings to create a public record of local government decisions in places that don’t have press coverage. The initiative has engaged more than 700 Detroiters and since spread nationwide, creating new opportunities for civic participation and public accountability.

What to Watch for in the 2026 U.S. Midterms

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-27 15:19 UTC

With the first U.S. midterm elections since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House approaching, voters will be weighing in on a range of issues, from the economy and rising cost of living, to the administration’s foreign policy and the future direction of both major parties. At a recent virtual Nieman-to-Nieman seminar, a group of Nieman alums who cover politics discussed what they’re hearing from voters with regards to key Senate races, the growing influence of younger voters drawn to progressive candidates, and the political implications of conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine, and Russia. Moderated by Austin Bogues (NF ’21), news desk editor at USA Today, the discussion brought together James Barragán (NF ’24), political anchor for Spectrum News in Austin, Texas; Bill Barrow (NF ’22), national politics reporter for The Associated Press in Atlanta; and Ines Pohl (NF ’05), Washington bureau chief and White House correspondent for Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster.

India Targets Journalists in Crackdown on Growing Protest Movement

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-19 21:20 UTC

As protests continue across India over allegations of government corruption, dozens of members of the media have been subjected to arrest, detainment and assault, according to witnesses, press rights organizations, and the journalists themselves. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi in recent weeks, demanding the resignation of election officials allegedly tied to the deletion of nearly 130 million names from voter registration rolls. The protests — which have largely been organized by the Cockroach Janata Party, so named after India's chief justice called the nation’s unemployed youth and activists "cockroaches" — are part of a wider wave of youth discontent aimed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. Organizers have mobilized young people via social media, tapping into frustrations with government corruption, eroding trust in democratic institutions, and a lack of access to jobs and educational opportunities.

Testing the Legal Limits of Press Access

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-15 14:51 UTC

The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the news media have followed a familiar pattern: President Donald Trump lashes out at news outlets for perceived bias and follows up with restrictive actions that appear blatantly unconstitutional; a judge’s ruling follows, temporarily halting the actions; and the administration pivots and pushes ahead with other restrictions. This time it was the removal of three outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from White House press access in September. After the groups sued, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their access on Sept. 24, the administration barred CNN and Politico from providing pool coverage on trips outside Washington. Kelly issued a longer, preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, halting the administration from blocking the news organizations’ access to the White House while the case proceeds. This Newsroom Wants You to Be Part of the Journey Before It Even Starts

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-06 10:00 UTC

My happiest times in journalism have been when I have built something new. For my latest venture, I want to help bring investigative journalism on climate and environmental issues to a much larger audience than it has reached in the past. To do so, I’m starting a brand-new newsroom focused on the environmental and climate crisis, and I’m taking my audience along for the ride. I’ll be documenting every facet of the process with an “open kitchen” approach of radical transparency, starting with a 100-day video countdown chronicling all the steps involved with starting a news organization from the ground up. This effort combines two of the things I’m most passionate about: I love digging up stories that other people don’t want to see published, and I love creating opportunities for other journalists. I’ve been a journalist for most of my life. I started working at age 14 for the local paper in my rural German town, turned to doing investigative stories in my early 20s, and later studied investigative journalism at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in New York.

America’s Shrinking Local Newsrooms, Through a Photographer’s Lens

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-02 12:30 UTC

For many journalists, the sight of empty desks is a sadly familiar one. My first glimpse of a gutted newsroom facing further cutbacks sparked a documentary photography project that has so far taken me to more than 50 newsrooms across the United States over the past eight years. It began when my mother, a loyal subscriber to our local metro in southern Illinois, told me a decade ago how disappointed she was in the newspaper. She complained that the local coverage was lacking, and the paper seemed to be thinner. Already several years into my photojournalism career, I was unsurprised by her remarks — I had been witnessing the decline of print media since graduation from journalism school. Still, my curiosity was piqued, and I arranged a visit to the paper to see for myself. Cue the scene of a barren newsroom. Not only were there empty desks, but also an expanse of exposed carpet with indentations showing where desks had once long stood. While there has been a great deal of reporting on the issues plaguing local journalism, I hadn’t seen the story told visually.

澳枪击事件嫌疑人为父子：曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”，行凶枪支为合法持有

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-16 02:23 UTC

据新华社12月15日援引澳大利亚广播公司报道，澳大利亚联合反恐小组调查人员表示，悉尼邦迪滩枪击事件两名嫌疑人曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”恐怖组织。 报道援引联合反恐小组一名不愿透露姓名的高级官员的话说，警方在邦迪滩两名枪手车内发现一面“伊斯兰国”旗帜。澳大利亚安全情报组织6年前就已在调查邦迪滩枪击案两名枪手之一的纳维德·阿克拉姆，他与“伊斯兰国”在悉尼的恐怖分子有密切联系。 澳大利亚警方表示，枪击事件的两名嫌疑人是父子关系，使用合法获得的枪支发动了此次袭击事件。 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯15日表示：“今天下午4点， 我将把更严格的枪支法律列入国家内阁的议程，包括限制个人可持有或许可的枪支数量 。此外，还需对许可证进行定期审查。人们的情况会发生变化，人们的思想也会随着时间的推移而变得激进。许可证不应永久有效。” 此次枪击事件已造成包括1名作案嫌疑人在内的16人死亡、40人受伤。这是自1996年塔斯马尼亚州亚瑟港枪击事件造成35人死亡以来，澳大利亚发生的最严重的大规模枪击事件。 持有枪支许可证长达十年 据多家外媒报道，其中一名袭击者为24岁的澳大利亚公民纳维德·阿克拉姆，他在现场被捕，随后被送往悉尼的一家医院。另一名袭击者是他的父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆，他于1998年来到澳大利亚，被警方当场击毙。 澳大利亚警方随后证实，纳维德·阿克拉姆此前已被新南威尔士州警方和其他机构记录在案。其父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆持有枪支许可证，名下登记有6支枪，目前均已被追回。新南威尔士州警察局长马尔·兰永透露，萨吉德·阿克拉姆已持有枪支许可证长达十年。 阿尔巴尼斯在新闻发布会上透露，纳维德·阿克拉姆曾于2019年10月首次引起当局的注意。他补充说，对该男子进行检查是基于他与其他人有联系，但评估结果表明，没有任何迹象表明他存在持续的威胁或暴力倾向。 新南威尔士州州长克里斯·明斯表示，警方正在调查他们的系统是否存在故障，导致合法持有的武器可能被用于恐怖袭击。 枪手“性格古怪”，爱好打猎 据《卫报》澳大利亚版报道，纳维德·阿克拉姆在袭击前从事砌砖工作。他的同事表示，纳维德性格古怪，“没人和他亲近”。“（砌砖工人）在一起的时间很长，因为砌砖是一项非常枯燥乏味的工作，所以大家会聊很多话。但纳维德是一个性格很古怪的人……他工作非常努力，几乎没有休息日。” 尽管澳大利亚警方并未确认纳维德·阿克拉姆是否合法持有枪支，但据这位同事表示，纳维德经常外出打猎，曾提及在昆士兰州南部高原的克鲁克韦尔附近射杀兔子和其他猎物。这位同事还表示，就在几周前，纳维德告诉老板，他的手骨折了，所以要到2026年才能工作。

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 14:23 UTC

在校园里，孩子们时常举起戴在手腕上的手表，彼此一碰，便加为好友。 这种以“安全”为核心卖点的儿童电话手表，如今已超越通信工具的属性，悄然演变成一个拥有独特规则、社交层级甚至灰色产业链的未成年人数字社交圈——“小天才圈”。 在这个属于他们的“江湖”里，“大佬榜”备受关注，“扩列”（增加好友）成为新的社交需求，“点主”（在主页点赞）是每日必做的功课……这些让成年人感到陌生的词汇，正构筑着未成年人的数字社交世界。 然而，伴随着这种社交形态的兴起，家长们的担忧也日益加剧：孩子过度沉迷手表社交、不良信息传播、因品牌壁垒导致的“社交绑架”等问题逐渐浮现。《法治日报》记者近日对该现象展开调查，试图揭开这一未成年人数字社交圈的真实面貌。 点赞成社交“硬通货” 据北京“小天才圈”资深玩家陈曦（化名）介绍，圈内有5000余名活跃用户，多为11岁至17岁的学生，这个社交圈形成了一套精心设计的“混圈规则”。“入圈”需设定两个字的独特圈名，随后可在平台分享生活点滴，吸引具有相同爱好的好友进行互动；若想提升知名度或影响力，需每日经营主页并与好友动态互动。 记者注意到，在一些社交平台上，大量以“小天才圈交友攻略”为主题的内容应运而生，内容涵盖如何快速“扩列”、获取更多点赞等“实用”技巧，评论区有不少“留下ID互加好友”的留言。在这一社交体系中，点赞是这套规则的核心——平台设定每日主页获赞上限为3000个，若要达到“100万+”的“大佬”级别，需连续点赞近一年时间。围绕点赞数与知名度，圈内形成了清晰的“大佬排行榜”，点赞数也成为社交“硬通货”。 这种对点赞的追逐，已催生出相关服务产业。记者调查发现，某社交平台上，拥有数十万甚至上百万点赞数的账号，售价从几百元到上千元不等：100多万点赞的账号标价1300元，90多万点赞的账号标价1200元。 今年18岁的“灵师”（圈名），在2021年14岁时加入“小天才圈”，她的账号目前已拥有150个好友、超100万点赞量。她告诉记者，这样的账号市场价值约1000元。 “围绕点赞需求，还衍生出代刷赞、租账号、出售‘大佬好友位’等服务。”“灵师”进一步介绍，例如付费100元至180元，即可获得“bot”（记者注：“bot”是一种第三方开发的自动化工具，主要用于刷赞、修改记录和发送动态等功能，这类工具能帮助用户快速提升账号点赞数，从而在未成年人社交圈中获得更高地位）自动点赞功能——用户将手表寄给相关人员进行10天左右的处理便能完成安装。此后，发帖5分钟内即可自动获赞，还可以一键查询未点赞名单。

产地造假、年份速成、无视监管！央视曝光新会陈皮市场乱象

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 08:23 UTC

近日，总台接到群众举报，反映陈皮市场存在年份虚标、产地及工艺造假等问题，千元一斤的“年份陈皮”亦可能名不副实。 茶枝柑新果皮冒充陈皮 广西浦北出现“速成工艺陈皮” 记者发现，直播间里售卖陈皮低价轮番轰炸，年份承诺掷地有声。 直播间也有主播爆料，八成市面上所谓广东新会陈皮实为广西陈皮。 广西钦州市浦北县是茶枝柑重要种植基地，其果皮是陈皮风味“越陈越香”关键，也是浦北陈皮唯一原料。2024年当地陈皮产业产值破60亿元，采收季大量鲜果加工晾晒成柑皮。 果农和收购商称，今年浦北茶枝柑鲜果收购价走低。按20斤鲜果出1斤柑皮比例，叠加人工成本，品相好的新柑皮成本约30元/斤，低端柑皮仅六七元，且当年新柑皮并非真正陈皮。 这家企业的负责人告诉记者，按行业共识与团体标准，柑皮需陈化三年以上才可称为陈皮，陈化时间越长价值越高，但他透露，自然陈化需长期积压资金，多数企业是难以承受的。 这家企业的负责人私下告诉记者，为缓解资金占用压力，一种名为“轻工艺”的速成加工方式，眼下正在部分陈皮生产企业里流行，他们仅需一个月的时间，就能将新采收的茶枝柑果皮处理为外观近似三年、五年自然陈化过的陈皮，这样做能大幅缩短陈化周期、降低企业的运营成本。 浦北自然陈化五年陈皮批发价每斤150元至200元，企业造假“工艺皮”成本仅70元左右，高额利润促使更多商家放弃自然陈化、铤而走险。 记者离开企业，在广西浦北县柑浦堂健康产业有限公司分拣车间，再次见到大批量造假“工艺皮”陈皮，同一批“工艺皮”因加工受热差异形成色差，被分拣标注为三年、五年等不同年份。 负责人透露，不同年份“工艺皮”本质相同，批发价均70元左右一斤，零售价差极大，标五年款卖500元一斤，标十年款卖1000元一斤，仅凭外观就能翻倍抬价，利润超成本十倍以上。 新会陈皮从浦北进货 “工艺皮”贴上陈皮标签以假乱真 浦北与新会陈皮原料同为茶枝柑，仅产地不同，新会较高生产成本使当地部分头部商家常年从浦北拿货，浦北成其重要原料供应地。 记者在柑浦堂分拣仓库看到，大量标注“新会陈皮”“新会特产”的纸箱正打包“工艺皮”，这些广西陈皮每日批量发往广东新会，造假供需链路已成熟稳定。 记者发现，浦北当地部分规模企业和小型收购商，已形成了这种“工艺皮”的造假供应体系，可自主加工或快速调配各类“年份”陈皮货品，个别企业年销新会原料数量惊人。 随后经浦北陈皮企业负责人引荐，记者见到多位专程从新会赴浦北采购的商家，他们坦言同时经营新会皮与浦北皮，外地“工艺皮”因价格低廉成电商供货重要选择。

《怦然心动》导演莱纳与妻子在家中遇害，警方尚未证实是其子所杀

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 07:23 UTC

当地时间12月14日，曾执导《怦然心动》《当哈利遇到莎莉》《危情十日》等影片的美国导演罗伯·莱纳（Rob Reiner）在他位于洛杉矶的家中遇害身亡。洛杉矶警察已对外证实，现年78岁的莱纳与他现年68岁的妻子米歇尔·辛格·莱纳（Michele Singer Reiner）的遗体一同被发现。 2019年，罗伯·莱纳（左一）与《当哈利遇到莎莉》的主演梅格·瑞恩、比利·克里斯托出席TMC经典电影节。 据悉，洛杉矶消防局的人员于当地时间12月14日下午3点38分接到医疗救助电话，赶赴位于布伦特伍德区的一处住宅中，随后发现两人已死亡。当天晚间，洛杉矶警察局在其社交媒体官方账号确认死者为导演罗伯·莱纳夫妇，将由抢劫凶杀部门主导调查。而好莱坞媒体TMZ援引执法部门消息称，“两人身上有与刀具造成的伤口相符的割裂伤。” 好莱坞媒体《每日野兽》称，有消息人士向他们透露，是两人的女儿罗米最先发现他们倒在血泊中；罗伯·莱纳当时已死亡，妻子米歇尔在救护车送院途中离世。 此外，《人物》杂志称通过多方消息，得知莱纳夫妇系被他们的儿子尼克（Nick）所杀害。不过，这一说法并未获得警方的证实。罗伯·莱纳与摄影师米歇尔·辛格相识于《当哈利遇到莎莉》拍摄时期，两人于1989 年结婚，育有三个子女，分别为杰克（Jake）、尼克（Nick）和罗米（Romy）。 2014年，罗伯·莱纳与妻子偕三名子女杰克、罗米、尼克（右三至右一）出席活动。 《人物》杂志还在报道中指出：尼克2016年接受其采访时，曾谈到自己长达数年的毒品成瘾经历。这段经历始于他十几岁出头，导致他一度流落街头。他表示，大约从15岁开始，便反复进出戒毒康复机构；随着成瘾问题不断加重，他逐渐与家人疏远，并在多个州经历了长时间的无家可归生活。 2025年9月15日，罗伯·莱纳在纽约出席活动。视觉中国 图 获取更多RSS： https://feedx.net https://feedx.site

演员何晴追悼会举行，其子追思母亲：北京这场雪像是为她而下

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 06:53 UTC

一场雪落，人间倩影化雪归天。 12月15日上午，众多剧迷粉丝冒着严寒赶到北京昌平殡仪馆久安厅，送别演员何晴最后一程。12月13日，这位被誉为“古典第一美人”的演员因病去世，终年61岁。 不到10点，殡仪馆告别厅外已经站满了前来悼念的观众和粉丝，有人胸前佩戴小白花，有人手捧鲜花，一位浙江的网友还托人送来了悼念花圈。 “何晴的作品在我们心中留下了太多美好回忆，她的演技和性格都让我们深深喜爱，这次听到她突然去世的消息，我们非常意外，来到这里也是一种悼念。”一位何晴的影迷说。 现场粉丝在悼念簿上写下对何晴的话，不到一会儿，悼念簿就已写满对她的怀念。一位观众用清秀的字迹写下：“亲爱的何晴，我们的童年、青春都在您的影视作品中得到陪伴。美丽可人的何晴，很痛心听到您的消息，我代表我的同学们来这为你送行。” 曾在电视剧《水浒传》中饰演卢俊义的演员王卫国也来到现场，神色哀切。他说自己和何晴既是邻居，也是多年好友，在他印象中何晴是一个温婉、暖心的人，没有架子，总是远远地和人打招，笑嘻嘻地说话。何晴生病时常给王卫国打电话，请他送自己去医院。即便病重时，何晴也保持乐观积极的态度，王卫国有些事情想不开，她还来开导自己。“何晴走了，我们都很难过。只要你记住她，她就永远还在。”王卫国说。 《水浒传》中卢俊义的扮演者王卫国 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青深情回忆何晴往事：“我们是小时候就认识的好朋友，从80年代到现在，有缘分做了这些年的朋友。她说话慢慢的，很甜很温柔。” 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青 在广大观众的真挚请求下，原本仅面向亲友的告别仪式临时对外开放，大家排着队，秩序井然地进入灵堂，与这位“荧屏中的温婉佳人、生活中的坚韧女性”做最后的道别。 久安厅内的屏幕上滚动播放着何晴的照片，厅内四周摆满了亲友的花圈，其中包括六小龄童、唐国强、翁虹、尤勇智等何晴圈内好友送来的花圈，还有《三国演义》剧组送来的花圈。人群中不时传来一阵抽泣。 何晴之子许何代表亲友致悼词。他回忆了何晴对抗病魔的乐观积极，以及作为母亲对孩子深深的爱和眷恋。 许何说，妈妈很喜欢下雪，经常在雪后穿一件毛茸茸的衣服外出赏雪。“今年12月12日北京下了第一场雪，我摸着妈妈的脸跟她说北京下雪了，下得好大，好像很久都没有下过这么大的雪。在我的心里，这场雪好像是刻意为她下的。12月13日早晨天空晴朗，白色的雪布满了大地，我妈妈在她最喜欢的早晨离开了大家，去了天国，远离了所有的疾病和痛苦。” 何晴，1964年1月13日出生于浙江衢州江山市。她是中国内地唯一一位演遍四大名著影视作品的女演员，被誉为“古典第一美女”。

Donors should fully fund the education programs, while Bangladesh should recognize and the United Nations should support a separate Rohingya-led school network. Humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps. But the programs, which aid cuts had shuttered for months in 2025, are barely adequate even for the children they reach and may close again, humanitarian officials told Human Rights Watch. newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

The geography of financial frictions

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-17 00:00 UTC

Firms’ access to external finance differs widely across Europe. This column uses data from the ECB’s Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises to map these differences and to study what they mean for monetary policy. The authors find that countries in which firms face tighter financial frictions respond less to the ECB’s monetary policy changes, and that they face a worse trade-off between output and inflation. A model of the monetary union suggests that financial integration in the spirit of the Savings and Investments Union would make monetary policy more effective, but potentially at a cost to financial stability.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Updating what workers learn: Technology, training content, and the supply of expertise

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-17 00:00 UTC

Raising educational attainment is the canonical way skills keep pace with technology. This column argues that changes in learning content matter just as much, drawing on five decades of legally binding German vocational training curricula linked to patents and administrative worker records. Occupational curricula more exposed to digital technologies are rewritten faster, mainly by adding new skills rather than discarding old ones. Entrants trained under the new content earn higher wages; older incumbents, who had completed the older curricula, see their wages fall.

Inside central banks’ currency portfolios: New evidence from 149 countries and 23 currencies

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-16 00:00 UTC

An increasing number of central banks have begun disclosing reserve currency shares. This column introduces a new public database providing information on the reserve currency composition of 149 countries across 23 currencies, covering the period 1999 to 2026, which allows a granular analysis of the factors driving reserve currency composition. Liquidity, return, and safety are the determinants most frequently cited when explaining allocation decisions. While central banks rarely acknowledge it publicly, a growing body of evidence also suggests a role for geopolitical considerations and international alliances.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Currency risk drives remittance fees as much as markups do

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-16 00:00 UTC

Senders now have more ways than ever to move money across borders, yet costs remain high and vary widely across corridors. This column argues that a missing piece in explaining these high costs is the exchange rate risk borne by the intermediaries that move the currency, the money transfer operators. Across 339 remittance corridors worldwide, fees rise when the recipient country’s currency becomes more volatile, and this currency risk adds about as much to the price of a transfer as operators’ markups. Competition alone cannot lower these costs.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

The effects of inflation on euro area public debt

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-16 00:00 UTC

Whether inflation can ease public debt burdens is an increasingly important question as debt sustainability concerns rise in the euro area. This column applies a new debt decomposition framework to assess how inflation affected debt ratios in the five largest euro area sovereign issuers over 2005–2025. It finds that inflation played a small role in reducing the public debt burden. The post-pandemic inflation surprise largely reflected imported costs, which do little to raise nominal output. Increases in longer-term inflation compensation lowered the market value of debt, but were not sufficient to offset the debt-increasing effect of earlier declines.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Growth alone is an unlikely fiscal saviour; resolving long-run fiscal tensions in OECD countries also requires expenditure restraint

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-15 00:00 UTC

In public discourse on fiscal tensions across OECD countries, the potential contribution of higher economic growth tends to be overstated. This column argues that long-run fiscal sustainability cannot prudently rely on growth alone. OECD modelling shows that under current policy settings, productivity-led growth provides minimal fiscal relief due to wage linkages, benefit indexation, and relative price effects. Growth from rising labour utilisation is fiscally more potent, but restraining public expenditure is the surest path to long-run fiscal sustainability.

How Will the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Affect Covered Entity Finances? -- by Charles J. Courtemanche

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative effect of switching to a rebate model.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Horizontal Equity of Taxation: Citizen Beliefs and Policy Preferences -- by Pierre Bachas, Christopher A. Hoy, Anders Jensen, Mahvish Shaukat

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Taxes are harder to enforce on the self-employed than on wage earners, creating horizontal inequities among taxpayers with similar incomes. Using tax microsimulation and household survey data from 29 developing countries, we show that horizontal inequities in actual tax systems are comparable in magnitude to vertical equity and are exacerbated by progressive reforms that fall disproportionately on wage earners. We then conduct surveys and randomized information experiments in Pakistan to study public perceptions of these inequities. Although providing information raises fairness concerns, it does not increase support for reforms reducing it, revealing an important political constraint to improving tax equity.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Monetary policy in a Phelps–Winter Economy -- by Bruce C. Greenwald, Joseph E. Stiglitz

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

We use the Phelps-Winter customer market—providing a better theory of price determination for large parts of the economy than the standard model—to show that raising interest rates induces higher prices, as firms value current profits more, and are more willing to lose customers for short-term gains. These inflationary effects can be significant in relevant ranges of interest rates; they exist in the short run even when interest rate hikes succeed in cutting aggregate demand; and that they are amplified by policy uncertainty and the uncertainty about the effects of interest rate changes, both of which have increased as conventional policy has demonstrably failed badly to keep inflation at the 2% target. Empirical studies confirm this low level of ineffectiveness of raising interest rates in reducing inflation.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Measuring the Impact of Impact Measurement -- by Emanuele Colonnelli, Timothy McQuade, Natalia Rigol, Benjamin N. Roth

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Impact measurement is central to impact investing and social entrepreneurship, yet little is known about whether firms benefit privately from measuring impact. We conduct the first randomized controlled trial of an impact measurement intervention among high-growth social enterprises in India. Treated firms exhibit nearly twice as much revenue growth and raise nearly twice as much capital as control firms. In a companion experiment with early-stage investors, we find that investors respond strongly to quantified impact metrics but not to generic qualitative impact statements. Together, our results show that impact measurement can shape firm growth and capital allocation.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Gambling for Goals -- by Costas Arkolakis, Spencer Y. Kwon, Dominic Russel, Claire Shi, Hyunjoo Yang

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Young adults in advanced economies have grown more pessimistic about their economic prospects in recent years. At the same time, gambling-like financial activities have proliferated. We link these trends through a Friedman-Savage (1948) motive: when life goals such as homeownership or marriage seem out of reach, individuals turn to financial gambles. We test this theory using an original survey combined with millions of linked records from Korea’s leading credit bureau, telecom provider, and credit card issuer. Consistent with the theory, individuals who place greater importance on hard-to-reach goals take more risk, and the form of risk they take varies systematically with their distance from those goals. Within individuals, cryptocurrency app usage rises during unemployment and falls after winning the right to purchase price-regulated housing through a lottery. A calibration shows how hard-to-reach goals lead households to act more aggressively on their beliefs, amplifying the consequences of overoptimism.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Investment and Governance: Through The Lens of Sustainability -- by Jitendra Aswani, Roberto Rigobon

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Using 3,944 sustainable bond issuances by public firms from 2013 to 2022, we examine the causal effect of sustainable investment on governance adoption. A heteroskedasticity-based identification strategy reveals that a 1% increase in sustainable debt (by total debt) raises the likelihood of sustainable governance adoption by 9.2%. Such adoption improves environmental performance by 16% (structural estimates). These effects are confined to non-financial firms; for financial firms, governance adoption alone is in-sufficient, as sustainable loan borrowers environmental performance does not improve. Firms with stronger environmental performance are less likely to adopt sustainable governance. Results are robust to alternative definitions and extensive specification checks.

Safety Cases Have an Agent Foundations Problem

LessWrong · 2026-11-17 04:29 UTC

If we want to ensure that AI systems are safe, should we approach the problem like an engineer, or a scientist? Do we need to discover deep and fundamental truths about how intelligence works, or is it better to focus our efforts on applying the battle-tested methods developed by safety engineers over the course of decades? As others have noted, this question is beginning to become a crux of disagreement between those who are concerned about the risks posed by advanced AI systems, and those who are relatively confident that humanity will muddle through. In this post I argue that it isn't clear how to use these safety engineering methods, or whether they work for advanced AI systems, because you immediately run into thorny scientific problems when you try to apply them. Furthermore, these thorny scientific problems are the same ones being studied under the banner of Agent Foundations. I'll start by laying out my understanding of how safety assurance typically works.

Empirical feelings

I often talk about feelings that I purportedly feel. ’That was fun!’, ‘I’m so glad this happened’, ‘I am overcome by sadness’. But a few years ago, in one of those discussions about transforming the known universe into optimal happiness substrate, it came to my attention that I didn’t really know what I was talking about with things like that. For one thing, I just wasn’t sure I knew what, for instance, anger characteristically felt like (in my defense, I’m usually distracted by some incredibly annoying thing happening whenever I am experiencing it). I could probably recognize anger, and was probably talking about it accurately when I said, ‘I am angry’. But if I tried to imagine anger when I wasn’t angry, I was not sure I got it right, and I didn’t have a good explicit description of it. But aside from that—whether or not I’m on top of what the famous feelings actually feel like—there is a question of whether the feelings I have are basically the ones people usually talk about.

Thoughts on "safety bad bc warning shots good"

LessWrong · 2026-11-17 02:33 UTC

Suppose there was a button which made the current generation of AIs more safe, i.e. more aligned and less capable of subverting control measures. The button has no other effects — in particular, the button wouldn’t make future generations more or less safe. Should you press the button? Maybe you shouldn’t, because of the Warning Shot Argument: Future agents contribute almost all the risk of catastrophe, compared with current agents. Pressing the button makes current agents safer. If current agents are safer, then they are less likely to cause non-catastrophic harms, e.g. cybercrime. If current agents don’t cause non-catastrophic harms, then people will be less aware about catastrophic risks, e.g. lab leadership, governments, legislators, international community, lab employees, general public, media, academia, etc. If people are less aware about catastrophic risks, then they won’t take drastic action to reduce catastrophic risk. So future agents contribute more catastrophic risk. Therefore pressing the button would increase catastrophic risk.

Listen: The imperfect world of pulsars

Big Think · 2026-11-14 07:08 UTC

Here in the Universe, there are a few things that are as close-to-perfect as can be. The Sun, for instance is the roundest object in the Solar System, but other stars are rounder, with white dwarfs and neutron stars exhibiting even more perfect roundness. Meanwhile, in terms of keeping time, we might think of the spinning Earth as a wonderful clock — after all, we base our calendar off of it — but the Earth spins down over time and changes its distance from the Sun: both factors that lead to it being rather imperfect as a timekeeper, especially over the long run. For keeping time, it turns out that the best natural clocks in the Universe are millisecond pulsars. It’s possible to look at a millisecond pulsar, measure its timing, and then look away for extremely long periods of time, like perhaps a year, and then when you return to it, know whether a billion pulses have elapsed or a billion-and-one pulses have elapsed.

Hence this modest proposal: If the European Union is serious about integration, it should get silly about names. All 12 of its major transnational economic corridors should be named after the bendy fruit. In other words, Europe should go full bananas. “Looks like a banana,” said the minister The Blue Banana — the first of the bunch, so to speak — is of surprisingly recent vintage. First proposed in 1989 by French geographer Roger Brunet as an economic zone with common characteristics, this urban-industrial belt runs from Manchester in northern England to Milan in northern Italy. A French minister remarked that Brunet’s area looked a bit like a banana, an illustrator for Le Nouvel Observateur colored it blue, and hey presto, the Blue Banana was born.

For thousands of years, humanity would wonder just what it was — at a fundamental, elementary level — that made up everything we saw, heard, or otherwise interacted with in the Universe. Ideas ran rampant early on, ranging from the notion of elements to a fundamental single root of everything to tiny building blocks composed of a variety of geometric shapes. It was only in the 19th century that we began breaking terrestrial matter down into the microscopic constituents that compose it, like molecules and atoms, that we began approaching the problem scientifically, and scientific progress continued into the 20th and now 21st centuries. Most of us learn in school about the existence of atoms, the different species of atom (known as elements), and the constituents of atoms: an atomic nucleus made of protons and neutrons, where the number of protons in the nucleus determines which element the atom is, and the much lower-mass electrons that orbit around the nucleus itself.

Scene Report | Summer Break in Mexico City

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-16 08:00 UTC

Scene Report is a series that explores a city's moviegoing culture over a month. Illustration by Angelo Dolojan. There are summers when Mexico City belongs to cinema. This was not one of them—it belonged to football. Months before the first whistle, sidewalks were being repaired with unusual urgency, facades were being repainted, metro stations acquired new signage, long-neglected public spaces suddenly became worthy of investment. Like every global mega-event, the FIFA World Cup arrived with the familiar rhetoric of urban renewal and international prestige. Whether those promises will outlast the tournament remains to be seen. What mattered during those weeks was that the city had accepted football as its temporary organizing principle. As someone who had deliberately decided to stay in Mexico City to experience the tournament, I surrendered without resistance. I have always loved football, and the chance to watch a World Cup unfold in my own city felt like a once-in-a-lifetime experience. During the tournament, everyday routines dissolved into celebration.

MUBI Podcast: Encuentros | “See Where No One Else Can”

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-13 22:12 UTC

In this episode, the conversation explores the relationship between imagination and reality, and the boundary between images and truth. Federico Luis is an Argentine filmmaker who has directed nearly ten documentary and fiction short films. In 2019, he presented La siesta in the Official Short Film Competition at the Cannes Film Festival, a section he recently returned to, winning the Palme d’Or for his documentary Para los contrincantes (2026), filmed in Mexico. In 2024, he premiered his debut feature, Simon of the Mountain, at Cannes Critics’ Week, where it received the Grand Prize. The film subsequently screened at several other international festivals, including San Sebastián, Havana, Cairo and Biarritz. Through a filmography that, in different ways, unsettles, distorts and expands reality, Luis explores how the freedom of fantasy can lend an air of mystery to the most ordinary situations.

Featuring Oscar-winner and Yol megafan Alejandro G. Iñárritu (Digger, 2026) and German-Turkish auteur Fatih Akin (Head-On, 2004). The MUBI Podcast returns for its 12th season, “Under Pressure.” At a time when artists worldwide are being threatened or stifled by their governments, host Rico Gagliano tells the stories of filmmakers from across history and around the world who have made movies in spite of incredible state pressure to compromise, give in, or give up. From 1970s Turkey to modern-day America, these are alternately wild, sobering, controversial, and inspiring tales of art by any means necessary.

The Possibilities of the Unseen: In Conversation with Lee Chang-dong

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-12 08:00 UTC

Lee Chang-dong. When I first met Lee Chang-dong in person, in April 2025, he was already waiting for me at his office in Seoul’s Mapo District. He sat hunched over his notes, reviewing the questions I had sent him in advance. After a moment of small talk, he looked up at me, his expression suddenly serious. “How long do you want to talk?” he asked. I thought two hours would be enough. “Not enough,” he replied. We talked for nearly four hours, with a large Secret Sunshine (2007) poster looming behind us. Our conversation took place in Seoul ahead of a retrospective of Lee’s work at Poland’s New Horizons Film Festival. He couldn’t attend in person, as he was busy finishing Possible Love (2026), his first feature since Burning (2018). When we met again this fall to continue our conversation after the premiere of his long-awaited return to cinema, I understood just how right he had been. One conversation had not been enough. Talking to Lee feels like reading an essay as it takes shape; his answers have the texture of carefully composed speech.

Mark Korven: Borderline Sonics and Dimensional Demarcation

The Wire Magazine · 2026-11-16 00:00 UTC

Mark Korven’s scores for The Black Phone (2021) and Them (2021) destabilise hermetic soundworlds to convey psychological violence, writes Philip Brophy in his latest Secret History of Film Music column The contribution of Canadian composer Mark Korven to contemporary horror cinema is aligned with composers who sculpt their scores through tactile manipulation. His self-built Apprehension Engine, a hybrid guitar-percussion instrument, empowers distinctive acoustic control. Korven commissioned Toronto based guitar maker Tony Duggan-Smith to build the modest box incorporating tools and techniques favoured by Korven: a hurdy-gurdy for cranking, a spring reverb for metallic resonance, metal rods and wooden tongues for bowing (similar to the waterphone), and a stretched wire for E-bowing. Its abject sonics pepper Robert Eggers’s The Lighthouse (2019) with terse shudders and emotional spikes, and are also audible in Adam Schindler and Brian Netto’s Don’t Move (2024).

To accompany his Global Ear feature in The Wire 514, Simon Coates compiles an annotated playlist of tracks from the Sri Lankan city Situated on Colombo’s Vauxhall Street, Musicmatters sits at the centre of the Sri Lankan city's experimental music world. “A lot of my introduction to experimentation in music came through Musicmatters around 2010,” says bass player Uvindu Perera. “I was new to it then, but these people were already listening widely and sharing references.” Simultaneously a collective, a school (Perera now teaches there), a record label and home to the Sound Room performance space, Musicmatters offers both an alternative to exam-heavy Western music education and provides space for explorations in sound as art and experimentation. Video: ZeN's Bakırköy Psychiatric Hospital concert, Istanbul, 1998

The Wire Magazine · 2026-11-10 00:00 UTC

Watch an exclusive clip of Turkish improv band ZeN’s Bakırköy Psychiatric Hospital concert from 1998 On 23 June 1998, Istanbul based experimental rock group ZeN performed at Bakırköy Psychiatric Hospital, following an invitation from two nurses who worked there. The musicians visited the hospital beforehand and decided to approach the performance with sensitivity to their audience while remaining true to their commitment to improvisation. At times, the lyrics seem to tell the story of the hospital and the concert itself, responding directly to the surroundings. The performance subsequently became one of the group’s most remarkable and cult recordings, released on cassette and CD in 1999 and reissued on vinyl in 2023. This exclusive edit with English subtitles is hosted by The Wire ahead of the release of a new documentary, ZeNistan, exploring the activities of ZeN throughout the 1990s.

culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · culture_probe

Against the Grain: Music criticism can become critical again – here's how

The Wire Magazine · 2026-11-09 00:00 UTC

Popular music criticism can become relevant again by situating itself in broader theoretical frameworks, argues Rafael Lubner in The Wire 514 These are lean times for popular music criticism. Negotiating a gutted publishing landscape, amid a Spotify-led devaluation of listening, the form finds itself under serious threat. One index of criticism’s attenuated state is the narrowing frame of reference employed by critics to apprehend musical objects – rarely do we find new works in the visual arts, film or literature employed to understand transformations in music’s sound or form. Take, as a point of comparison, Greg Tate’s recently reissued Flyboy In The Buttermilk (reviewed in The Wire 513). Here are passionate defences of Miles Davis’s earth-shaking mid-1970s funk odysseys alongside surveys of Afrodiasporic art and reviews of writer Nathaniel Mackey and literary critic Henry Louis Gates Jr. Contemporary music criticism, by contrast, seems resolutely committed to understanding music as siloed from the non-musical.

By revitalizing a neglected canal, we created a fresh and vibrant urban environment and planned a continuous and open public space along the waterfront. Lambda House is located on the southeastern edge of the urban center of Castellvell del Camp, where the consolidated residential fabric gives way to the agricultural fields of the Picarany Ravine. This transitional setting, slightly removed from the urban continuity, establishes a direct visual relationship with the landscape, granting the house a peripheral yet connected position to the natural environment. The area is characterized by medium-sized plots of diverse shapes, mostly occupied by single-family homes with gardens, resulting from urban development that expanded between the late 20th and early 21st centuries in the intermediate space between Reus and Castellvell del Camp.

Spirit Crossing, the new Zelda-ish hangout MMO from the creators of Cozy Grove, understands that sometimes you just want to be alone

Rock Paper Shotgun · 2026-11-16 17:59 UTC

New multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together. Read more

AI ‘slop’ is a social judgement

Nature Human Behaviour · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02639-6 Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content increasingly saturates our information environment. Efforts to detect and remove it are failing. We propose that calling AI-generated content ‘slop’ is best understood as a social judgement: what a community recognizes as unwanted AI content. Studying AI slop this way makes it tractable, measurable and governable.

There’s New Hope for Detecting Alzheimer’s Before Cognitive Deficits Manifest

Nautilus · 2026-11-16 21:00 UTC

With no cure for Alzheimer’s on the horizon, and our best treatments only slowing the progression of the disease, there’s been an intense effort to find earlier means of detection. Now, a new study published in Neuroimage Reports is offering hope of diagnosis even before cognitive symptoms become noticeable. A team of biomedical imaging specialists, pathologists, and neuroscientists from Johns Hopkins University studied how the brains of older adults changed over time by analyzing hundreds of MRI scans and PET scans. They relied on longitudinal data from two different studies (the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study) that included people from across the Alzheimer’s spectrum, from cognitively healthy to full-blown dementia. Evaluation of Lassa fever surveillance system in Edo State, Nigeria (2024–2025)

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-16 14:00 UTC

by Paul Waliaula Wekunda, Oladipo Ogunbode, Zainab Dambazau, Oyeladun Okunromade, Musonda Chikwanda Introduction Lassa fever is a priority disease in Nigeria. Periodic evaluation of its surveillance systems is essential to strengthen performance and ensure efficient use of limited public health resources. This study evaluated the Lassa fever surveillance system in Edo State, Nigeria. Methods The evaluation followed the 2001 CDC guidelines and used a cross-sectional mixed-methods design. We reviewed statewide surveillance data from 2024–2025 and selected respondents from 26 health facilities across 15 of the 18 (83.3%) local government areas (LGAs), as well as from the state surveillance unit and WHO. We assessed the surveillance system’s evolution, structure, and resource availability. We analyzed surveillance data by person, place, and time and audited the data for completeness, errors, outliers, and timeliness. Case investigation forms, laboratory forms, and line lists were reviewed to assess variable usefulness and identify data gaps.

by Marcelo Luis Urquia, Maria Paula Godoy, Carolina Fonseca Leal de Araújo, Carla Adriane Leal de Araújo, José Roberto da Silva Junior, João Guilherme Bezerra Alves Background Child marriage, defined as a legal marriage or informal union of a minor, is considered a violation to human rights and is associated with adverse developmental and health outcomes. Brazil is one of the countries with the highest number of child marriages worldwide. In 2019, Brazil enacted legislation banning child marriage for <16-year-olds. We examined the time trends in child marriage before and after the law and contextualized them within those of adolescents and young adults up to 24 years of age. Methods We accessed public-use anonymized marriage and birth registrations nationwide data in the period 2014–2024, with complete information on age and marital status. To describe the trends before and after the law reform, we used interrupted time series analysis. Analyses were stratified by age (<16, 16–17, 18–19 and 20–24 years), marital status (legally married and informal unions) and sex.

Detectability of controlled leaks in an Andean water transmission main: A field evaluation of changepoint methods on flow and pressure signals

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-16 14:00 UTC

by Holger Manuel Benavides-Muñoz, Peter Cheung Leak detection on pumped transmission mains that cross steep terrain relies on hydraulic signals whose response to a small leak may be comparable to sensor noise. We evaluated five unsupervised methods (PELT with Bayesian and Akaike penalties, Bayesian online changepoint detection [BOCD], an OLS-CUSUM structural-break procedure and a moving-average ±3σ chart) on flow and pressure series recorded every 30 s during seven controlled leak trials (valve setting 3–5% of nominal flow) in two field campaigns on an Andean transmission main in Loja, Ecuador. Detections were compared with a chance-level reference obtained by placing the same number of changepoints at random. Relative to the preceding leak-free observations, flow decreased in all seven trials (mean −0.50%; sign test p = 0.016; placebo test p = 0.003), whereas pressure, recorded at 0.1-m resolution, showed no change (placebo p = 0.99). No single event exceeded its per-event detection threshold; the flow change was resolvable only as a seven-event mean (signal-to-noise ratio −3.3).

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-16 14:00 UTC

by Grace W. Auckley, Jordan M. Marshall The Grand Sable Dunes is a perched lacustrine dune system within Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore, USA, on Lake Superior. Wind provides disturbance which has continually influenced the successional pathways of these dunes. The objectives of this study were to identify the relationships between forest stand age, successional processes, and overall forest development by categorizing forest type and regeneration patterns, mapping the dendrochronological sequence, and quantifying coarse woody debris (CWD) accumulation in the Grand Sable Dunes. We surveyed the understory, midstory, and overstory woody vegetation across 43 plots. Cores from the four largest trees were collected and CWD volume was measured within each plot. Results indicated that there is a chronosequence across the dunes that is supported by forest type, stand age, and CWD. There was a positive relationship between distance from shore and midstory and overstory diversity, stand age, and CWD accumulation.

Black holes remain some of the most mysterious and awe-inspiring celestial objects ever studied. This primarily comes from the fact that they literally can’t be observed unless they interact with something in its surrounding environment, most notably a star. llm 0.37.3

Simon Willison's Weblog · 2026-11-16 23:57 UTC

Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code. Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp: That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm, webassembly, sqlite, generative-ai, ai, llms, d-richard-hipp

The Greatest Car Stunt Was Also The World’s First Computer-Modeled Stunt

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

owl writes: https://boldentrance.com/astro-spiral-the-greatest-car-stunt/ The corkscrew car jump in The Man With The Golden Gun is the coolest car stunt in any movie series. Following Bond tradition, the car stunt was done for real. No models or computer trickery. Well, to be honest, a computer was used but not in the way you might expect. This famous 1974 jump of an AMC Hornet X over a twisted, broken bridge was the first car stunt, or any stunt for that matter, to be extensively computer-modeled. As you can imagine, making this car perform a barrel roll in midair and land on the other side on its wheels is pretty complex. The twisted ends of the bridge have to be elevated at just the right angle, the car has to hit the bridge at just the right speed, and perform the airborne barrel roll at just the right moment to ensure an elegant and safe landing. In a stunt like this, safety is top priority, but making Bond look good is also important. Gödel's Notebooks in Obscure Shorthand Contain Myriad of Novel Proofs

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

JoeMerchant writes: https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/13/kurt-godel-notebooks-ai-helps-unlock-hidden-discoveries-man-who-transformed-maths With the help of Claude model LLM agents and the proof assistant Coq, logician Jan von Plato uncovered 663 theorems obscured in Kurt Gödel's 1940s shorthand notebooks, including roughly 400 verified proofs and 200 repairable ones. Most notably, the analysis revealed that Gödel was just one step away from proving the independence of the axiom of choice—a foundational breakthrough in set theory that later earned Paul Cohen the 1966 Fields Medal. Beyond confirming Gödel's past claims, the workbooks contain dozens of results that anticipated mathematical developments of the 1970s and 1980s, along with 14 entirely unexplored themes in logic and the foundations of mathematics. These discoveries build on Gödel's legacy of transforming modern mathematics and computation, demonstrating how his systematic, idea-driven proofs laid groundwork that researchers are only now beginning to explore.

"Arthur T Knackerbracket" writes: ISO working group faces a fight over runtime checks, complexity, and the language's release timetable: The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature. Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup, who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language. datasette 1.0a43

Simon Willison's Weblog · 2026-11-15 23:20 UTC

Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone, which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory: private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0. A new Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai, Peter Olkhovets, Ilya Khalafi, and Ankita Advitot.

Announcing XRAID: declustered parity RAID for zoned XFS

LWN.net · 2026-11-13 14:39 UTC

Christoph Hellwig has announced the initial public release of XRAID—declustered parity RAID that is integrated into XFS. The two primary aims of XRAID are to support parity RAID on zoned devices like SMR hard drives, and to provide a fast RAID implementation without inherent data integrity problems. XRAID, just like zoned XFS also works on conventional hard drives and SSDs. Optimizing for SSD performance has not been a focus, but even without that, writes are up to 20 times faster than mdraid. [...] Work on XRAID has been ongoing for a year and a half, and while we aren't anywhere near ready for an upstream submission, we are interested in feedback and testing from a wider audience now. The current implementation supports zero to 2 parities. We did experiments with the SnapRAID parity library to support 3 and more parities, and while that is not included in the current version, support for more parities is planned and the code is prepared for it. The xfsprogs branch includes mkfs support and a new "xraid" utility for managing devices and inspecting an XRAID file-systems.

specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Bliki: Generated Glossary

Martin Fowler · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances. The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations generate enough text to do the job. The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the most confusion.

Bliki: LLM Voice

Martin Fowler · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”.

Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-11-16 18:35 UTC

The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a service proxy implementation with better performance than the iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API, and the ipvs backend was never able to implement all of the edge cases of Kubernetes Service functionality correctly. In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33. Part of the plan behind adding the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace both the iptables and ipvs backends. Because the ipvs backend in particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it as of Kubernetes 1.35. Although it currently remains available in kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly. That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change. That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-27 04:30 UTC

We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standard Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions.

On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.

A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed. The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it. Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.

Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run.

The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-06 18:00 UTC

In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1 Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.

Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-05 18:00 UTC

Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost.

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

IEEE Spectrum Robotics / IEEE Spectrum · 2026-11-16 14:00 UTC

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die. Can Agentic Robotics Solve Robotics’ Data-Scaling Problem?

IEEE Spectrum Robotics · 2026-11-09 14:00 UTC

Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do. There are even robotics companies that exist solely to collect training data and sell it to other robotics companies in pursuit of this goal. But whether data will finally bring us general-purpose robots is an open question. Nobody knows how much data would be necessary, what kind of data is important, or whether something else might be missing. And there are other problems with a reliance on massive amounts of data: The resulting AI algorithms are essentially black boxes, which despite their high performance are difficult or impossible for humans to understand. This characteristic is becoming increasingly concerning in commercial deployments, where robots must be flexible, reliable, and safe.

Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left. The skies are becoming dangerously crowded—not with planes but with interference and jamming disrupting many of the 30,000 radio frequencies that civil aviation relies upon. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Spectrum · 2026-11-13 19:00 UTC

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges. “AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance. Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

This White Paper explains how ice, wind and vegetation load overhead distribution lines at the same time. It shows engineers how to assess the complete line and compare resilience options. What you will learn about: How freezing rain, rime ice and wet snow add weight to conductors and change their shape in the wind. Why a moderate wind on a heavily iced line can govern design, and how galloping and vegetation contact create outages. How a messenger-supported spacer cable separates the electrical function of covered conductors from the main mechanical load path. How monitored severe-weather test data compares tension changes in bare, covered and spacer cable systems. What utility records from the December 2008 Northeast ice storm show about circuit availability and restoration. How to compare options at corridor level, check the full load path of poles, brackets and foundations, and apply energized-line safety rules. Download this free whitepaper now!

EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework

Electronic Frontier Foundation · 2026-11-16 22:50 UTC

The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches. Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred.

Donate Equity to Support Digital Rights: Stocks, DAFs, and Giving

Electronic Frontier Foundation · 2026-11-16 20:23 UTC

Do the holidays have you thinking about how you can support your favorite nonprofit? For 35 years, the Electronic Frontier Foundation has been advancing our digital rights, including defending security researchers, encrypting the web, and fighting illegal surveillance. Donating equity to EFF can help support this important work. Perhaps your family has taken advantage of the new tax law around giving by creating a Donor-Advised Fund. Perhaps your employer has gone public and you now own stock. Perhaps you’ve seen some of EFF’s recent successes and thought, Man, imagine what they could do with more. Stocks A gift of equity can help your contribution go farther and offer tax savings. When you donate appreciated stock, you avoid paying capital gains tax on any increase in its value. You also receive a charitable income tax deduction for the fair market value of appreciated stock on the date it is transferred. Also, more and more companies are offering gift-matching programs that can double your impact at no additional cost.

Amazon Ring’s New Indoor Surveillance Drone Is Not Compatible with Privacy

Electronic Frontier Foundation · 2026-11-16 17:58 UTC

Amazon Ring has finally announced their long-dreaded indoor drone, a small flying surveillance device connected to their security suite of products that can fly around your house filming and recording things. The device is supposedly designed to fly preset paths across your home and will also activate if a sensor or alarm has been triggered. Customers should think twice about purchasing these devices for a number of reasons. These devices are problematic in many of the ways we’ve said Ring’s stationary home surveillance products are a problem, plus some new ways. At a very basic level, they are essentially a window into your house that can be accessed by anyone with access to your account—which has historically included bad actors looking to embarrass or harass Ring users and employees of the company. What’s worse, Ring has supercharged the units with its ‘AI Pilot’ to map routes, model the interior of the home, and control movement. This means not only is the footage being sent to corporate servers, but the company is also making inferences about your home to carry out tasks.

Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again)

Electronic Frontier Foundation · 2026-11-13 21:29 UTC

Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did. Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants, rings, and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long. Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps, collaborative software, or your cloud backup solutions, have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are all now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game.

This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop. I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing. I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. Penlink’s Webloc is an application that locates people using information from the weather, gaming, email, and religious apps on their phone. It’s sold to the police. Law enforcement officers can use Webloc to zero in on a map and look at all phones that were present at a specific place and time, analyzing “billions of location data points,” according to company documents reviewed by Bloomberg...

🤕 Medicare's AI Experiment | EFFector 38.20

Electronic Frontier Foundation · 2026-11-11 18:32 UTC

When we need medical care, we expect decisions about our treatment to be made by our doctors, not a tech company's algorithm. But in January, the federal government launched a program that uses AI to evaluate Medicare beneficiaries' requests for certain procedures. EFF sued for records on WISeR, seeking badly needed transparency about Medicare's AI experiment. In our latest EFFector newsletter, we're talking about what happens when the government outsources treatment approval to private AI companies—without sufficient transparency, testing, or legal limits. JOIN OUR NEWSLETTER For over 35 years, EFFector has been your guide to understanding the intersection of technology, civil liberties, and the law. This issue covers unconstitutional digital dragnets, a post office surveillance scheme, and what EFF uncovered about Medicare's AI experiment. Prefer to listen in? EFFector is now available on all major podcast platforms.

We’re Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches

Electronic Frontier Foundation · 2026-11-09 22:09 UTC

Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Image: Low-tech Magazine Volume IV (2022-2026). Photo: Juliette Demaret. Low-tech Magazine presents the fourth volume in the chronological book series. It contains twenty articles that were published online between 2022 and 2026. Three earlier volumes collect articles written and published online between 2007 and 2021, which are also bundled in the “Compressed Edition”. This new volume is a bit different from the earlier books: eight of the articles are DIY guides or manuals, and we have grouped them together in the second part of the book. This volume covers the period that Marie Verdeil joined Low-tech Magazine, which partly shifted the focus from writing articles to building prototypes inspired by historical research. These prototypes also led us to conduct workshops in universities and participate in museum exhibitions. As is the case with all of our books, the articles have been edited and improved compared to the original web versions. Some articles gained extra or better images.

specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe

Rediscovering the Handcart

Low-Tech Magazine · 2026-04-22 00:00 UTC

Image: The handcart, equipped with a sail. Photo by Kris De Decker. The human-powered handcart is the oldest of vehicles, and it will likely be the last one around in the future. Of all vehicles, it’s the cheapest and least complex to build and use. It offers a large advantage over carrying a load on your back or dragging it over the ground - the even older concept of the sled. On the other hand, the handcart is cheaper and easier to use than the animal-powered cart. Oxen and donkeys eat more than humans, and they have their own will, which can work against the driver. Like any other wheeled vehicle, the handcart requires roads to drive on. This infrastructure has not always been available anywhere or at any time in history. For example, in medieval Europe, porters and pack animals were more common than handcarts because of poor roads. 1 In the West, the handcart only reached its heyday during the first decades of the Industrial Revolution, when it connected fast-growing cities to train stations and harbors.

specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe

Low-tech Magazine: The Uncompressed Book Series

Low-Tech Magazine · 2026-03-30 00:00 UTC

Image: The redesigned and revised chronological book edition. Photo: Marie Verdeil. Between 2019 and 2021, Low-tech Magazine published three books containing selections of articles from the website, spanning 14 years (2007-2021). In 2024, we launched the “compressed edition”, which squeezes the article catalog of the three-volume book series into just one book of 620 pages. We did this by switching to a smaller font size, downsizing most images, and opting for a two-column layout. I rewrote some articles, especially older ones, resulting not only in fewer pages but also in better articles. This revised edition of the original, “uncompressed” series is based on the edits made for the compressed edition. However, we increased the font and image sizes and returned to a one-column layout for improved reading comfort. The book design is a collaborative effort by Laia Comellas, Marie Verdeil, and Johanna Gratzer. Marie Verdeil made the covers, Vaiva Vinskaitė did the typesetting. Image: The redesigned and revised chronological book edition. Photo: Marie Verdeil.
